strengths: The paper addresses a useful NLP deployment question: how much labelled data makes task-specific training preferable to prompting larger models. Studying performance crossovers provides more practical guidance than comparing only zero-shot and full-data endpoints.
The experimental coverage is substantial: eight datasets, eight model families, four adaptation/inference approaches, varying training sizes, and quantized versus non-quantized comparisons.

Repeated evaluation—100 runs for fine-tuning, 20 for most other approaches, and 10 for GPT—is a valuable strength. Reporting learning curves and standard deviations exposes variation that single-run comparisons would miss.

The manuscript provides prompts, verbalizers, major training settings, individual-model plots, and a source-code link. It also explicitly acknowledges limitations concerning prompt choice, English-only evaluation, test subsampling, and possible contamination.
weaknesses: The headline average of 100 labelled samples is not adequately derived. Table 1's fine-tuning crossover points average 680 samples against prompting and approximately 1,941 against in-context learning. An aggregate including instruction-tuning could differ, but its construction and weighting are unspecified. Report reproducible summaries separately by specialization method and comparator, explain how missing crossovers are handled, and align the title and annotation recommendations with those results.

The variance-adjusted criterion in Section 3 does not establish the claimed 'worst-case' performance or a calibrated probability of superiority. Subtracting one standard deviation from one mean and adding it to another provides a descriptive separation rule. A reliability claim requires an explicit probability target and appropriate analysis of paired performance differences or empirical quantiles, including uncertainty in the estimated crossover. Changing test splits and subsampling evaluation for larger models also mix evaluation noise with training and demonstration-selection variability.

The prompting baselines require validation. Table 2's BoolQ instruction asks whether the passage contains an answer, whereas BoolQ requires answering the question with yes or no. The SNIPS verbalizer 'Musing' also needs clarification. Furthermore, one prompt engineered on Mistral is reused across models. These choices can materially disadvantage general models and shift the central crossovers; task-faithful prompts, documented output-to-label mapping, and checks across multiple valid prompts are needed.

Model selection and annotation accounting are insufficiently specified. Appendix A.2 reports the best shot counts and precision variants, while the main figures select the best model, without clearly identifying whether these choices use validation or test performance. The 20% validation split and early stopping may also require labels beyond the advertised training budget. Specify the selection protocol, account for labels used in selection and stopping, and evaluate selected configurations on common held-out examples.

Experimental descriptions conflict in a way that impedes reproducibility. Section 3 and Appendix A.2 describe varying available label budgets, but Appendix D states that large-model prompting and in-context learning were evaluated only at a 1,000-label setting. Clarify the demonstration pools, which conditions were actually run, and how the learning curves were constructed. Exact size grids and crossover extraction procedures are also needed. These uncertainties affect the central comparisons and prevent a sound Findings recommendation in the current form.

The efficiency and quantization conclusions exceed the evidence. Table 3 supplies one approximate FLOP value per approach without a sufficiently specified workload, including training size, token lengths, and inference volume; this does not establish comparable computation across the experiments. Figure 6 also shows roughly a 25–30 macro-F1-point quantization loss for Zephyr on BoolQ, which warrants substantial qualification of the 'minimal impact' conclusion.

Explanations involving dataset characteristics, model size, and contamination remain exploratory. Class count, task type, architecture, and training history vary together. Section 3.1 invokes pretraining exposure to explain LLaMA-3's SNIPS behavior, although the Limitations section acknowledges that exposure is unknown. These explanations should be presented as hypotheses, and the broad recommendations about an 'optimal' approach should be restricted to the supported experimental conditions.
